finding.statement: Scoring every non-zero candidate against the fifteen attributes on a five-level scale - strong, soft or partial, unknown or untested, absent, contradicted - puts Candidate B, Ackworth, Cheddington 1608, C(ii) Berkhamsted, Candidate D, the Epping and North Weald line, Hitcham, the Newgate apprentice, Weston Turville, the Bucks/Herts/Beds group, A(1603) Stewkley, Gurley of Westminster, C(i) Berkhamsted and Stewkley 1611 side by side, with the eliminated Eythorne household scored as calibration. Laying them out side by side is what made the structural finding visible; it was not apparent from any candidate's own file. The three leading probability rows - no record survives or is indexed anywhere, documented but never assembled into a person, and documented but in a source or class not yet searched - are not people and cannot be scored on the matrix at all, and between them they hold about 44 percent.

finding.statement: Every candidate for the Braintree emigrant is tested against a single specification of what the man and his household must look like, stated as fifteen attributes, each a scale rather than a binary and none of them mandatory: the surname Gurney or a variant; a household containing Mary, Richard and/or John Jr. in that order; a Mary born about 1628; a Richard born about 1630; a John born about 1633; a father named John; a mother named Mary; the father born about 1603; a John-and-Mary marriage about 1622-28; alternatively a John-and-Mary marriage about 1628-40 under a second-marriage hypothesis; the father's own father named Richard; a region known for Great Migration participation; a region connected to Weymouth, Massachusetts or the colonial John's cohorts; the father a tailor; and an event about 1636-39 whose context could support emigration, read throughout as a documented push event. Holding the specification separate from any candidate's own evidence is what makes the candidates comparable at all.
